title: A multinational monopolizes school cafeterias in Andalusia amid complaints from families about food quality
text: A multinational monopolizes school cafeterias in Andalusia amid complaints from families about food quality The deficiencies in a public service increasingly outsourced by the regional government have already led to a user strike and a disciplinary proceeding. A multinational that already manages nearly half of the 1,445 outsourced Early Childhood and Primary School cafeterias in Andalusia is dominating the complaints from families at public schools in the region due to the poor quality and lack of variety in the meals. A multinational company is dominating the school cafeterias in Andalusia, sparking complaints from families about the poor quality of the food. The deficiencies in this public service, which has been increasingly outsourced by the regional government, have already led to a user strike and a disciplinary proceeding. Mediterránea dominates Andalusia school cafeteriasThis multinational, which already manages nearly half of the 1,445 outsourced Early Childhood and Primary School cafeterias in Andalusia, is at the center of many complaints from families at public schools in the region due to the poor quality and lack of variety in the meals. The parent associations attribute this situation to the progressive outsourcing of a public service that has ended up in the hands of just nine companies responsible for feeding thousands of children.Complaints from families of students at public schools in the provinces of Córdoba, Granada, Málaga, and Seville have been mounting against the multinational, which employs over 12,000 people and serves 800 centers across Spain, Portugal, and Latin America, preparing 300,000 meals daily. The company was acquired by the Swedish fund EQT in March.Mediterránea has significantly increased its presence in Andalusia, going from managing 478 school cafeterias in 2023 (34% of the total tendered) to 606 currently (42%), nearly double the number of school cafeterias managed by the Andalusian regional government itself, according to a report by the organization. This contract has a total value of nearly 100 million euros (specifically 97.8) for the period up to the 2027-2028 school year.This is a service that this year feeds approximately 188,000 students and to which the regional government dedicates a budget of 97 million euros per year. While slightly more than 300 cafeterias operate under direct administration, over 80% are in private hands, and this number is shrinking as the system has gone from 21 companies exploiting the service in 2019 to just nine, according to the study.The accumulation of services in a few companies, in a region the size of Portugal, means the food is usually prepared in centralized industrial kitchens and delivered twice a week in plastic containers to be reheated. This catering system, called \"cook and chill,\" was the most criticized by families in a 2023 survey of nearly 4,000 people, cited in the report.Córdoba families protest food qualityComplaints about the food quality provided by Grupo Mediterránea have been centered in the province of Córdoba, where more than 20 schools supported a strike on October 23 organized by parent associations. One of these was the Noreña School, where a protest was held for three days after receiving 105 complaints in just three weeks about the food quality.\"The famous video of the school cafeteria in Galicia is a reality here in Córdoba,\" says Ángela Pulido, representing the parent association, which is part of the center's dining commission, to which over 200 students are enrolled. The supermarket sets the table and competes for the daily menu with the restaurant: prepared dishes, cheaper, and ready to eat, is a concept she uses to criticize the low quality of the food served in the school cafeteria.\"They served a pumpkin cream first and then lentils with vegetables. The lentils were not inedible, but for a child who is given legumes and vegetables three days out of five, well, you see,\" she recounts, finding it suspicious that macaroni is planned for the three Mondays that are holidays in Córdoba in October and November, effectively removing it from the school menu.The food from the central industrial kitchen in Málaga arrives at the school twice a week, on Mondays and Wednesdays, and is then heated every day before serving. The quality gap between the public and private sectors is stark: while families at the Noreña public school pay 5.54 euros, students at private subsidized schools in Córdoba, with fees slightly higher, enjoy a much higher quality meal prepared daily in the school's own kitchen.\"We don't demand anything out of this world. If some schools already have it and we also deserve it, why don't we have it?\" asks Pulido. Fátima López, spokesperson for the AMPA at another public school in Córdoba, Julio Romero de Torres, also points to the poor quality, citing \"mushy\" carrots that the kids call \"worms\" and \"rubber-like\" chicken. She notes that the multinational has not responded to the complaints in writing. The regional government is also investigating the service quality in Córdoba.Official investigation into catering servicesThe Andalusian Ombudsman, Jesús Maeztu, announced yesterday that he is processing a complaint from the parent associations about the quality of the meals in the province and that the regional government is conducting inspections. The spokesperson for Mediterránea stated that they cannot make statements while the investigation is ongoing, but they are \"collaborating with the Andalusian authorities\" and are committed to \"improving the service.\" Meanwhile, the companies continue to profit. The study reveals that the nine companies that manage over 80% of the school cafeterias in Andalusia reported revenues of 8.8 billion euros in 2023, with a net profit margin ranging from 4.6% to 9.6%. The authors of the report conclude that the regional government has failed to control the quality of the service after its privatization and that the current tender model allows \"excessive profits\" for the companies.The report suggests that public-public cooperation between the regional government and city councils could be a more efficient alternative for managing the service.
summary: A multinational monopolizes school cafeterias in Andalusia amid complaints from families about food quality The deficiencies in a public service increasingly outsourced by the regional government have already led to a user strike and a disciplinary proceeding.
